nameStory: The "glaucous" in this gull's name comes from the Latin word for gray-blue, describing its distinctive pale coloring that sets it apart from darker gulls. An older English name for this impressive bird was "burgomaster," suggesting its commanding presence among other seabirds—like a mayor ruling over the harbor!
description: The Glaucous Gull is a massive, pale gray and white seabird—actually the second-largest gull species in the world. These Arctic visitors are notably bigger and bulkier than the common gulls you see at beaches, with a thick, powerful build and broad wings. Adult birds have very pale gray backs and wings with pure white wingtips (no black markings), while their heads, necks, and underparts are clean white.

idTips.label: Pale wingtips
idTips.description: The wingtips are completely white or very pale gray—never black like most other large gulls. This ghostly pale appearance is visible both in flight and when the bird is perched.

idTips.label: Massive size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and bulkier than Herring Gulls, with a thick neck and broad chest that gives them an imposing, almost hawk-like silhouette when perched.

idTips.label: Overall pale coloring
idTips.description: The entire bird appears washed-out or bleached compared to other gulls, with very light gray on the back and wings contrasting with bright white elsewhere.

idTips.label: Heavy yellow bill
idTips.description: Large, thick yellow bill with a slight hook at the tip and often showing a red spot on the lower part. The bill looks proportionally massive compared to smaller gulls.

idTips.label: Pink legs
idTips.description: Sturdy pink or flesh-colored legs that appear thick and powerful, supporting the bird's substantial weight when walking on ice or rocky shores.

habitat: Along New England's rocky coastlines, harbors, and fishing ports during winter months, often near fishing boats and fish processing facilities. They prefer areas with access to both open water and ice, frequenting piers, breakwaters, and coastal dumps where they can scavenge for food.

seasonality.spring: Most individuals begin heading back to Arctic breeding grounds, though some may linger into early spring. Look for birds in transitional plumage showing mixed adult and immature features.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during summer months, as adults are busy breeding in the high Arctic. Any summer sightings are likely non-breeding individuals or birds unable to migrate north.
seasonality.fall: First arrivals from the Arctic begin appearing in late fall, often showing up at fishing ports and harbors as ice begins forming further north.
seasonality.winter: Peak viewing season when these Arctic visitors are most common along the coast. Adults show their cleanest white and pale gray plumage during this time.

funFact: Glaucous Gulls are such powerful predators that they regularly hunt and eat other seabirds, including murres, kittiwakes, and even other gulls—they've been observed swallowing whole puffins and can crack open thick-shelled eggs with their massive bills!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Iceland Gulls, which are also pale with white wingtips, but Iceland Gulls are noticeably smaller with more delicate features and longer, thinner wings. Remember: Glaucous = Gigantic and robust, Iceland = slender and elegant.
contextualKnowledge: These birds are true Arctic specialists that breed further north than almost any other gull species, which explains why they're such rare and exciting winter visitors to New England—seeing one is like getting a postcard from the top of the world.
compareHints: Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller. The similar Iceland Gull shares the white wingtips but has a much more delicate build and smaller head, making the Glaucous Gull look like the heavyweight champion of the gull world.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
